definition: searching widely for food or provisions
memoryTip: For-aging: out aging in the wild hunting for food.
correctPassage: The documentary follows bears foraging for salmon along the river.
wrongPassages: The committee spent the morning foraging the budget line by line.
After the storm, the marina looked foraging with every slip empty.
She offered a foraging compromise neither side could fully accept.

definition: in a way not directly expressed; understood without being stated
memoryTip: Im-plied, not said out loud — understood between the lines.
correctPassage: By remaining silent, the board implicitly endorsed the chair's decision.
wrongPassages: He searched implicitly by opening the first result and never scrolling.
She argued implicitly by shouting the same claim over every objection.
The lecturer spoke so implicitly that every syllable was easy to transcribe.

definition: a natural liking or sense of connection
memoryTip: A-finity: a natural 'fit' — you click with someone or something.
correctPassage: She felt an immediate affinity for the spare, geometric style of the paintings.
wrongPassages: He stored the affinity next to the spare batteries in the utility closet.
The clerk stamped affinity on the passport and waved her through customs.
They measured the room's affinity with a laser tape before ordering shelves.

definition: division into parts; a wall or screen that divides space
memoryTip: Part + ition — splits a whole into parts, or the wall that does it.
correctPassage: A temporary partition divided the gallery into two smaller exhibition rooms.
wrongPassages: Tuesday navigation to pin partition was a habit without any real purpose.
He finally opened the lock using a key from the old partition drawer.
The chef plated the dessert with a careful partition of mint on top.

definition: very skilled or proficient at something
memoryTip: A-dept: depth of skill — you're really good at it.
correctPassage: She is adept at turning dense research into clear public explanations.
wrongPassages: The marina looked adept in winter with every slip left empty.
Managers hoped to adept call transfers by removing the transfer button.
The empty parking lot felt strangely adept after the festival packed up.

definition: cheerfully optimistic, especially in a difficult situation
memoryTip: From Latin sang (blood) — rosy-cheeked and upbeat when things look grim.
correctPassage: Despite the delays, the director remained sanguine about the opening date.
wrongPassages: The remix felt sanguine because the key and tempo had both shifted.
Critics called the finale sanguine for its abrupt, unresolved ending.
The coda's sanguine motif belonged in an entirely different symphony.

definition: existing only in theory or as an idea; hypothetical
memoryTip: Only a notion — theoretical on paper, not yet real.
correctPassage: The budget included only a notional amount for travel until costs were known.
wrongPassages: He set the severity to notional after legal review had already escalated it.
The station's notional gate display counted down to a train that never came.
Voters rejected the notional levy that schools said would prevent layoffs.

definition: sleepy; tending to induce sleep
memoryTip: Slumber = sleep — anything slumberous makes you drowsy.
correctPassage: The heat and the soft music had a slumberous effect on the audience.
wrongPassages: Fans called the remaster slumberous for crushing dynamics with loudness.
The courtroom grew slumberous as lawyers traded sharp, rapid objections.
She treated the deadline as slumberous and worked straight through the night.

definition: having the ability to restore health, strength, or well-being
memoryTip: Restores you — rest or care that puts energy back.
correctPassage: A weekend by the lake proved restorative after months of deadline pressure.
wrongPassages: The plaza design was restorative: benches faced away from one another.
She closed the incident report as restorative before any interviews began.
The terminal's restorative art wall was a vinyl wrap of another airport.

definition: to make information known; to give a quality to something
memoryTip: Im-part: pass along a part of knowledge or a quality.
correctPassage: Good mentors impart not only techniques but also habits of careful reading.
wrongPassages: He tried to impart the sealed filing by posting it on a public forum.
The monitor will impart escalations by looping them into an unread channel.
She hoped to impart the walkout by docking the planning lunch as unpaid.

definition: not justified or authorized; lacking good reason
memoryTip: No warrant — no justification; not called for.
correctPassage: The criticism was unwarranted; the study had carefully controlled for bias.
wrongPassages: An unwarranted border crossing still requires passports, checks, and stamps.
The bog hollow stayed unwarranted after every free-running ditch lowered it.
His unwarranted limitation clause ran longer than the rest of the contract.

definition: unreasonably high in price or amount
memoryTip: Ex-orbit: way outside the orbit of a fair price — too high.
correctPassage: Residents complained about the exorbitant fees charged by the utility company.
wrongPassages: Her exorbitant testimony contradicted itself on both times and names.
Critics called the live-stream mix exorbitant for chat audio over the music.
The witness gave an exorbitant account that left out every key detail.

definition: to set or mark the boundaries of something
memoryTip: De-mark a line — draw the borders clearly.
correctPassage: A stone wall was built to demarcate the boundary between the two farms.
wrongPassages: She hoped to demarcate the mutiny by deleting the chat history overnight.
The cron job will demarcate SLA breaches by rewriting the SLA mid-month.
The bot will demarcate the ticket by closing it with 'thanks!' and no fix.

definition: able to be understood; clear enough to grasp
memoryTip: You can 'get' the intelligence of it — understandable.
correctPassage: Even without technical training, the diagram makes the process intelligible.
wrongPassages: Voters defeated the intelligible levy that schools said would prevent cuts.
The epilogue was intelligible: it opened a sequel instead of closing the story.
The floodplain stayed intelligible behind a levee raised after the last crest.

definition: careful judgment; freedom to decide as one sees fit
memoryTip: Discreet judgment — careful choice, or the power to choose.
correctPassage: Hiring decisions are left to the manager's discretion within stated guidelines.
wrongPassages: The permit titled discretion had a gold seal and no operative language.
The crate stamped discretion held bubble wrap and nothing else of value.
Routing code discretion bounced every message straight to the mailroom floor.

definition: modesty; freedom from showiness or pretension
memoryTip: Not pretentious — simple and real, no showing off.
correctPassage: The café's unpretentiousness—plain tables, no music—was part of its appeal.
wrongPassages: She wrote unpretentiousness as a bullet and never returned to fill it in.
The sticker book treated unpretentiousness as a gold star for participation.
The recipe listed unpretentiousness next to salt as if it were an ingredient.

definition: to become less intense, severe, or active
memoryTip: Sub + side: sink down — a storm, fever, or anger calms.
correctPassage: Once the fever began to subside, she was able to sleep through the night.
wrongPassages: The snow cornice felt subside behind a seasonal fence and warning signs.
Historians labeled the decade subside once the archives left little in doubt.
Trustees cut the subside arts grant that local schools had already matched.

definition: a mischievous practical joke
memoryTip: A playful trick — fun until someone gets hurt or mad.
correctPassage: What started as a harmless prank escalated into a costly misunderstanding.
wrongPassages: The team hoped to prank reopen rates by locking closed tickets forever.
The bog hollow stayed prank after drains lowered the entire water table.
Viewers found the remake prank for matching the original runtime exactly.

definition: to show or reveal a quality, feeling, or trait clearly
memoryTip: E-vince like evidence — it shows a quality is there.
correctPassage: The early drafts already evince the precision that would mark her mature style.
wrongPassages: She practiced the speech evince until every pause landed the same way.
The alliance was evince: both sides published the full text of every clause.
The decree stayed evince until translators agreed on one English version.

definition: to make impossible; to prevent from happening
memoryTip: Pre-clude: close the door in advance — make it impossible.
correctPassage: A prior commitment precludes her from joining the evening session.
wrongPassages: They tried to preclude the sinkhole by filling it with loose, uncompacted trash.
He moved to preclude the deposition by claiming he did not recall any facts.
She tried to preclude the relapse by returning at once to the same triggers.
